title: Enable custom exception types for workflow failures (NVIDIA-AI-Blueprints/aiq)
raw_text:
Enable custom exception types for workflow failures — open-source issue in NVIDIA-AI-Blueprints/aiq. Labels: good first issue. 
**Custom exception types for workflow failures.**
In `@src/aiq_agent/agents/deep_researcher/agent.py` 

Lines 215 and 234 raise `ValueError` for runtime workflow failures (no markdown output, no valid citations). These are not programming errors but legitimate failure modes of the LLM-driven workflow. Custom exception types (e.g., `WorkflowOutputError`, `CitationValidationError`) would:
1. Allow callers to distinguish workflow failures from actual programming errors
2. Enable more precise

title: [Bug] Manual /compact errors "Compaction requires a configured LLM model" for model-less SDK harnesses (openai-agents, pi, goose, qwen, copilot) (omnigent-ai/omnigent)
raw_text:
[Bug] Manual /compact errors "Compaction requires a configured LLM model" for model-less SDK harnesses (openai-agents, pi, goose, qwen, copilot) — open-source issue in omnigent-ai/omnigent. Labels: Bug, help wanted, comp:server, comp:web-ui, comp:harnesses, P2-medium, triaged. ### Description

The web-UI `/compact` control is exposed for **all** harnesses (it's a built-in slash command, not harness-gated). For SDK-style harnesses that have **no dedicated runner `/compact` handler** — `openai-agents` / `open-responses`, `pi`, `goose` / `goose-native`, `qwen` / `qwen-native`, `copilot` — the control falls through to a `204`, so the **server** runs its AP-side compaction (`_run_compact_locked`). When the agent spec pins no model (neither `executor.model` nor `llm.model`)
summary: this open-source bug highlights an issue in a system designed to manage different ai models or "harnesses." some harnesses, like those for openai agents, might not have their own built-in llm configuration. when a general "compact" function (perhaps for optimizing or summarizing data) is called, the system incorrectly expects an llm to be configured, leading to an error. it's about how different ai components interact and are managed within a larger framework. understanding such bugs is vital for mlops and sde roles, teaching you about system design, error handling, and the complexities of integrating various ai models and sdks. when building your own multi-model or agent-based system, think about how each component's dependencies and configurations are handled, especially for shared functionalities.

title: content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string (lastmile-ai/mcp-agent)
raw_text:
content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string — open-source issue in lastmile-ai/mcp-agent. Labels: bug, good first issue. use home assistant as mcp server,  then Calling OpenAI ChatCompletion with messages,  but the content in message is a list structure.

OpenAI API Specification：
- content can only be a string or null.
- It cannot be a list, object, or any other type.

If content is a list,  some LLM(deepseek) return the following error:
`[mcp_agent.workflows.llm.augmented_llm_openai] Error: Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: messages[2]: invalid type: sequence, expected a string at line 1
summary: this open-source issue points out a common problem when interacting with apis: data type mismatches. specifically, it notes that the `content` field within messages sent to openai's chatcompletion api is expected to be a string or null, but in this particular agent system, it's being sent as a list. this discrepancy causes errors, especially when other llms (like deepseek) are used, as they strictly adhere to the api specification. it's a fundamental bug in how data is structured and passed. for sde/swe/aiml roles, understanding api specifications and ensuring correct data types is fundamental to building robust systems that integrate with external services. when working with any api, always consult its official documentation for data types and expected formats. pay close attention to error messages, as they often pinpoint such issues.
why: highlights critical importance of api data type adherence for robust llm integrations.

title: Grading the Grader: Lessons from Evaluating an Agentic Data Analysis System
author: Tian Zheng, Kai-Tai Hsu
raw_text: Agentic data analysis systems produce rich outputs, including code, numerical results, and verbal diagnostics. This makes them more challenging to evaluate than single-turn LLM responses. It is therefore necessary to distinguish genuine disagreement between an agent's output and a ground-truth answer from grading artifacts. We investigate how reliably automated graders assess such a system and what strategies improve grading quality by applying LAMBDA, a multi-agent data-analysis system, on 153 numerical QRData tasks from DSGym. We develop and evaluate a three-layer human-AI grading cascade: strict regex matching, LLM-based lenient grading, and snippet-based human inspection, which combines non-GenAI and GenAI strategies with different failure profiles. Both automated graders achieve 100% observed precision (0/70 false positives). The lenient grader's recall is 97% against human labels. A keyword-anchored extraction pipeline raises the strict grader's recall by 60 percentage points over a last-number heuristic; the lenient grader is architecturally parser-independent. An iterative nudge mechanism raises grading run success from 36% to 97% and lenient-pass rates from 16% to 46%; comparing nudging with and without original-question re-injection shows that re-injection offers no benefit, confirming the nudge as an answer template cue. We further observe in this case study that variable type is the task metadata field most consistently associated with grading pipeline dynamics and observed outcome grades.
summary: this paper explores the challenges of evaluating agentic data analysis systems, which are more complex than simple large language model (llm) responses because they produce varied outputs like code, numbers, and text. it highlights that distinguishing genuine errors from grading artifacts is difficult. the research investigates how reliably automated graders can assess such systems and suggests strategies to improve grading quality, using a multi-agent system called lambda as a case study. for you, as someone interested in agents and llms, understanding these evaluation complexities is crucial. when you build your own agentic systems, you'll need robust ways to measure their performance beyond basic metrics. try to think about how you would objectively evaluate an agent that generates multiple types of outputs for a complex task.
why: teaches how to reliably evaluate complex agentic ai systems, crucial for your agent development.

title: [Good First Issue] Add Docker Compose for full-stack local development (Climate-Vision/ClimateVision)
raw_text:
[Good First Issue] Add Docker Compose for full-stack local development — open-source issue in Climate-Vision/ClimateVision. Labels: good first issue. ## Overview
New contributors currently have to manually piece together how to run the full stack (FastAPI backend + React frontend + GEE credentials). A `docker-compose.yml` would let anyone spin up the entire application with one command.

## Scope
- [ ] Create `Dockerfile` for the Python backend (multi-stage: builder + runtime)
- [ ] Create `Dockerfile` for the React frontend (nginx serve static build)
- [ ] Create `docker-compose.yml` with services:
  - `api` — FastAPI backend
  - `frontend`
summary: This open-source issue is a great opportunity to learn about and contribute to full-stack development using docker compose. The project, climate-vision, currently requires new contributors to manually set up its various parts – a fastapi backend, a react frontend, and google earth engine credentials. Docker compose simplifies this by allowing you to define and run multi-container docker applications with a single command. This means all the different services of an application (like your database, backend, and frontend) can be spun up consistently and easily, making development and testing much smoother. It's crucial for efficient team collaboration and deploying applications. You could try to set up a simple full-stack application (e.g., a python backend and a react frontend) using docker and docker compose to understand its benefits firsthand.
